queries.cypher:
MATCH (tc:TargetCompany)-[:FACES_RISK]->(r:Risk)
WHERE toLower(r.name) CONTAINS 'profit' OR toLower(r.description) CONTAINS 'profit' OR toLower(r.why) CONTAINS 'profit' OR toLower(r.source_text) CONTAINS 'profit'
WITH tc, collect(properties(r)) AS target_risks
OPTIONAL MATCH (peer:Company {is_peer:true})-[:COMPETES_WITH]->(tc)
OPTIONAL MATCH (peer)-[:FACES_RISK]->(pr:Risk)
WHERE toLower(pr.name) CONTAINS 'profit' OR toLower(pr.description) CONTAINS 'profit' OR toLower(pr.why) CONTAINS 'profit' OR toLower(pr.source_text) CONTAINS 'profit'
WITH tc, target_risks, peer, collect(properties(pr)) AS peer_risks
RETURN tc.name AS company, target_risks, peer.name AS peer, peer_risks
LIMIT 300

MATCH (tc:TargetCompany)-[:HAS_METRIC_CATEGORY]->(mc:MetricCategory)-[:HAS_METRIC]->(m:Metric)
WHERE mc.name = 'Profitability'
OPTIONAL MATCH (peer:Company {is_peer:true})-[:COMPETES_WITH]->(tc)
OPTIONAL MATCH (peer)-[:HAS_METRIC_CATEGORY]->(pmc:MetricCategory {name: mc.name})-[:HAS_METRIC]->(pm:Metric)
WHERE pm.label = m.label AND pm.year = m.year
WITH tc, peer, mc, m, collect({name: pm.name, label: pm.label, xbrl_tag: pm.xbrl_tag, value: pm.value, year: pm.year}) AS peer_metrics
RETURN tc.name AS target, peer.name AS peer, mc.name AS category, m.name AS target_metric, m.label AS target_label, m.xbrl_tag AS target_tag, m.value AS target_value, m.year AS year, peer_metrics
LIMIT 300

{"source_page": 14, "section_title": "Item 1A.  Risk Factors", "source_text": "The Company operates in very competitive industries, which could adversely affect our profitability.

The Company has many competitors. Some of our principal competitors have greater financial and other resources than we have. Accordingly, these competitors may be better able to withstand economic downturns and changes in conditions within the industries in which we operate and may have significantly greater operating and financial flexibility than we do. We also face competition for some of our products from alternative products, and some of the competition we face comes from competitors in lower-cost production countries like China and India. As a result of the competitive environment in the markets in which we operate, we currently face and will continue to face pressure on the sales prices of our products from competitors, which could reduce profit margins.

The Company’s sales could be adversely affected by consolidation in customer industries.

Several consolidations in the paper industry have taken place in recent years and such consolidation could continue in the future. These consolidations could result in partial or total closure of some paper mills where the Company operates satellite plants. Such closures would reduce the Company’s sales, except to the extent that they resulted in shifting paper production and associated purchases of calcium carbonate to another location served by the Company. Similarly, consolidations have occurred in the foundry and steel industries. Such consolidations in the major industries we serve concentrate purchasing power in the hands of a smaller number of manufacturers, enabling them to increase pressure on suppliers, such as the Company. This increased pressure could have an adverse effect on the Company’s results of operations in the future.

The Company’s sales could be adversely affected by our failure to renew or extend long-term sales contracts for our satellite operations.

The Company’s sales of calcium carbonate to paper customers are typically pursuant to long-term evergreen agreements, initially ten years in length, with paper mills where the Company operates satellite plants. Sales pursuant to these contracts represent a significant portion of our sales in the Specialty Additives product line of the Consumer & Specialties segment. The terms of many of these agreements have been extended or renewed in the past, often in connection with an expansion of the satellite plant. However, failure of a number of the Company’s customers to renew or extend existing agreements on terms as favorable to the Company as those currently in effect, or at all, could have a substantial adverse effect on the Company’s results of operations, and could also result in impairment of the assets associated with the satellite plant.

Financial Risks

Servicing the Company’s debt will require a significant amount of cash. This could reduce the Company’s flexibility to respond to changing business and economic conditions or fund capital expenditures or working capital needs. Our ability to generate cash depends on many factors beyond our control.

At December 31, 2024, the Company had $971.3 million aggregate principal amount of total indebtedness (consisting primarily of $575.0 million aggregate principal amount of loans under our term facility, $400.0 million aggregate principal amount of notes and $4.5 million outstanding under our revolving credit facility) and an additional $386.4 million of borrowing capacity under the revolving credit facility (after giving effect to $9.1 million of outstanding letters of credit). Our outstanding indebtedness will require a significant amount of cash to make interest payments. Further, the interest rate on a significant portion of our borrowings under our senior secured credit facility is based on SOFR interest rates, which has resulted in and could continue to result in higher interest expense in the event of continued increases in interest rates. Our ability to pay interest on our debt and to satisfy our other debt obligations will depend in part upon our future financial and operating performance and upon our ability to renew or refinance borrowings. Prevailing economic conditions and financial, business, competitive, regulatory and other factors, many of which are beyond our control, will affect our ability to make these payments. We cannot guarantee that our business will generate sufficient cash flow from operations or that future borrowings will be available to us in an amount sufficient to enable us to fund our liquidity needs. If we are unable to generate sufficient cash flow to meet our debt service obligations, we will have to pursue one or more alternatives, such as reducing or delaying capital or other expenditures, refinancing debt, selling assets, or raising equity capital. Further, the requirement to make significant interest payments may reduce the Company’s flexibility to respond to changing business and economic conditions or fund capital expenditure or working capital needs and may increase the Company’s vulnerability to adverse economic conditions.

{"source_page": 15, "section_title": "Item 1A.  Risk Factors", "source_text": "The agreements and instruments governing our debt contain various covenants that could significantly impact our ability to operate our business.

The agreement governing our senior secured credit facility and the indenture that governs our 5.0% Senior Notes due 2028 contain a number of significant covenants that, among other things, limit our ability to: incur or guarantee additional indebtedness, pay dividends or make other distributions or repurchase or redeem capital stock, prepay, redeem or repurchase certain debt, issue certain preferred stock or similar equity securities, make loans and investments, sell or otherwise dispose of assets, incur liens, enter into transactions with affiliates, enter into agreements restricting our subsidiaries’ ability to pay dividends and consolidate, merge or sell all or substantially all of our assets. In addition, we are required to comply with specific financial ratios, including a maximum net leverage ratio, under which we are required to achieve specific financial results. Our ability to comply with these provisions may be affected by events beyond our control. A breach of any of these covenants would result in a default under the applicable agreements. In the event of any default under our senior secured credit facility, our lenders could elect to declare all amounts borrowed under the credit agreement, together with accrued interest thereon, to be due and payable. In such an event, we cannot assure you that we would have sufficient assets to pay debt then outstanding under the credit agreement, the indenture governing our notes, and any other agreements governing our debt. Any future refinancing of the senior secured credit facility is likely to contain similar restrictive covenants. We may also incur future debt obligations that might subject us to additional restrictive covenants that could affect our financial and operational flexibility. We cannot assure you that we will be granted waivers or amendments to these agreements if for any reason we are unable to comply with these agreements or that we will be able to refinance our debt on terms acceptable to us, or at all.

Technology, Development and Growth Risks

The Company’s results could be adversely affected if it is unable to effectively achieve and implement its growth initiatives.

Sales and income growth of the Company depends upon a number of uncertain events. Growth will depend in part on sales growth from our existing businesses and customers. The Company has a strategic growth initiative to increase penetration into geographic markets such as Brazil, India and China as well as other Asian and Eastern European countries. The Company also has a strategic growth initiative to increase penetration into consumer-oriented markets such as pet litter, personal care, and oil purification. Our strategy also anticipates growth through future acquisitions. However, our ability to identify and consummate any future acquisitions on terms that are favorable to us may be limited by the number of attractive acquisition targets, internal demands on our resources and our ability to obtain financing. Our success in integrating newly acquired businesses will depend upon our ability to retain key personnel, avoid diversion of management’s attention from operational matters, and integrate general and administrative services. In addition, future acquisitions could result in the incurrence of additional debt, costs and contingent liabilities. Integration of acquired operations may take longer, or be more costly or disruptive to our business, than originally anticipated, and it is also possible that expected synergies from future acquisitions may not materialize. We also may incur costs and divert management attention with regard to potential acquisitions that are never consummated. Difficulties, delays or failure of any of these strategies could affect the future growth rate of the Company.

Delays or failures in new product development could adversely affect the Company’s operations.

The Company’s future business success will depend in part upon its ability to maintain and enhance its technological capabilities, to respond to changing customer needs, and to successfully anticipate or respond to technological changes on a cost-effective and timely basis. The Company is engaged in a continuous effort to develop new products and processes in all of its product lines. Difficulties, delays or failures in the development, testing, production, marketing or sale of such new products could cause actual results of operations to differ materially from our expected results.

The Company’s ability to compete is dependent upon its ability to defend its intellectual property against inappropriate disclosure, theft and infringement.

The Company’s ability to compete is based in part upon proprietary knowledge, both patented and unpatented. The Company’s ability to achieve anticipated results depends in part on its ability to defend its intellectual property against inappropriate disclosure and theft as well as against infringement. In addition, development by the Company’s competitors of new products or technologies that are more effective or less expensive than those the Company offers could have a material adverse effect on the Company’s financial condition or results of operations.

{"source_page": 17, "section_title": "Item 1A.  Risk Factors", "source_text": "The Company relies on shipping bulk cargos of bentonite from the United States, Turkey and China to customers, as well as our own subsidiaries, and we are sensitive to our ability to recover these shipping costs. If we cannot secure our container requirements or offset additional shipping costs with price increases to customers, our profitability could be impacted. We are also subject to other shipping risks. In particular, rail service interruptions have affected our ability to ship, and the availability of rail service, and our ability to recover increased rail costs, may be beyond our control. In addition, governmental restrictions can, and during the COVID-19 pandemic did, affect our ability to ship our products.

Operational Risks

The Company’s subsidiaries, BMI Oldco Inc. (f/k/a Barretts Minerals Inc.) (“Oldco”) and Barretts Ventures Texas LLC (together with Oldco, the “Chapter 11 Debtors”), have filed voluntary petitions for relief under Chapter 11 of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code to address and comprehensively resolve Oldco’s liabilities associated with talc. Risks and uncertainties related to this filing could have a material adverse effect on the Company’s business, financial condition, results of operations and cash flows.

The Company and certain of the Company’s subsidiaries are among numerous defendants in over six hundred cases seeking damages for alleged exposure to asbestos-contaminated talc products sold by the Company’s subsidiary Oldco. On October 2, 2023 (the “Petition Date”), notwithstanding the Company’s confidence in the safety of Oldco’s talc products, the Chapter 11 Debtors filed voluntary petitions for relief under Chapter 11 of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Texas (the “Chapter 11 Cases”) to address and comprehensively resolve Oldco’s liabilities associated with talc. Minerals Technologies Inc. and the Company’s other subsidiaries were not included in the Chapter 11 filing. In the second quarter of 2024, Oldco sold its talc assets under section 363 of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code.

In addition, in the second quarter of 2024, the Company entered into a Debtor-in-Possession Credit Agreement with Oldco (the "DIP Credit Agreement") and recorded a provision for credit loss of $30 million for the maximum aggregate principal amount under such DIP Credit Agreement.

Proceeds of the sale of Oldco's talc assets and funds drawn by Oldco under the DIP Credit Agreement will be used to fund the Chapter 11 Cases. The Chapter 11 Debtors' ultimate goal in the Chapter 11 Cases is to confirm a plan of reorganization under Section 524(g) of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code and utilize this provision of the Bankruptcy Code to establish a trust that will address all current and future talc-related claims. In January 2024, the Chapter 11 Debtors and Minerals Technologies Inc. commenced a court-approved mediation process with the Official Committee of Unsecured Creditors (appointed in the Chapter 11 Cases as the representative of current talc claimants)

(the “Committee”)

and the Future Claimants Representative (appointed in the Chapter 11 Cases as the representative of future talc claimants) regarding the terms of a potential consensual plan of reorganization and the ultimate amount to be contributed to any trust. The mediation process is ongoing. During the pendency of the Chapter 11 Cases, the Company anticipates that the Chapter 11 Debtors will benefit from the operation of the automatic stay, which stays ongoing litigation in connection with talc-related claims against the Chapter 11 Debtors. In addition, subject to certain exceptions, the filing or continued prosecution of all talc-related claims against the Chapter 11 Debtors' non-debtor affiliates is temporarily stayed through April 15, 2025 (subject to further extensions), the date on which a hearing is scheduled on the status of the Chapter 11 Cases. The Chapter 11 Debtors have been deconsolidated from the Company’s financial statements since the Petition Date.

Although the Chapter 11 Cases are progressing, it is not possible at this time to predict how the Bankruptcy Court will rule on the Committee’s motion to dismiss the Chapter 11 Cases, the form of any ultimate resolution or when an ultimate resolution might occur. Accordingly, the amount that will be necessary to fully and finally resolve all of Oldco’s current and future talc-related claims in connection with a confirmed Chapter 11 plan of reorganization cannot be estimated at this time. Several risks and uncertainties related to the Chapter 11 Cases could have a material adverse effect on the Company’s business, financial condition, results of operations and cash flows, including the ultimate amount necessary to be contributed to any trust established pursuant to Section 524(g) of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code, the potential for the Company’s talc-related exposure to extend beyond

the Chapter 11 Debtors

arising from claims by talc plaintiffs relating to the Company’s liability for talc claims, corporate veil piercing efforts or otherwise, any final resolution of the scope of the Pfizer indemnity, the ongoing costs of the Chapter 11 Cases, which may require additional funding from time to time, the cost and the length of time necessary to ultimately resolve the cases, either through settlement or as a result of litigation arising in connection with the Chapter 11 Cases, and the possibility that the Chapter 11 Debtors will be unsuccessful in attaining relief under Chapter 11. Further, while the Company anticipates that

the Chapter 11 Debtors

will benefit from the operation of the automatic stay during the Chapter 11 proceedings, depending on the ultimate outcome of any of these litigation matters, the Company could in the future be required to pay significant amounts as a result of settlements or judgments, potentially in excess of liabilities accrued to date in respect of such matters. The resolution of, or recognition of additional liabilities in connection with, pending or future litigation could have a material adverse effect on the Company’s results of operations, cash flows and financial condition.

For a further discussion of the Chapter 11 Cases and Oldco's talc-related liabilities, see Note 17 to the Consolidated Financial Statements, included in this report.

{"source_page": 18, "section_title": "Item 1A.  Risk Factors", "source_text": "The Company is subject to stringent regulation in the areas of environmental, health and safety, and tax, and may incur unanticipated costs or liabilities arising out of claims for various legal, environmental and tax matters or product stewardship issues that could materially harm the Company’s results of operations, cash flows and financial condition.

The Company’s operations are subject to international, federal, state and local governmental environmental, health and safety, tax and other laws and regulations. We have expended, and may be required to expend in the future, substantial funds for compliance with such laws and regulations. In addition, future events, such as changes to or modifications of interpretations of existing laws and regulations, or enforcement polices, or further investigation or evaluation of the potential environmental impacts of operations or health hazards of certain products, may affect our mining rights or give rise to additional compliance and other costs that could have a material adverse effect on the Company. Further, certain of our customers are subject to various federal and international laws and regulations relating to environmental and health and safety matters, especially customers of our Environmental & Infrastructure product line of our Engineered Solutions segment, who are subject to drilling permits, waste water disposal and other regulations. To the extent that these laws and regulations affecting our customers change, demand for our products and services could also change and thereby affect our financial results. State, national, and international governments and agencies have been evaluating climate-related legislation and regulation that would restrict emissions of greenhouse gases in areas in which we conduct business, and some such legislation and regulation have already been enacted or adopted. Enactment of climate-related legislation or adoption of regulation that restrict emissions of greenhouse gases in areas in which we conduct business could have an adverse effect on our operations or demand for our products. Our manufacturing processes for our products use a significant amount of energy and, should energy prices increase as a result of such legislation or regulation, we may not be able to pass these increased costs on to purchasers of our products. We cannot predict if or when currently proposed or additional laws and regulations regarding climate change or other environmental or health and safety concerns will be enacted or adopted.

The Company is also subject to income tax laws and regulations in the United States and various foreign jurisdictions. Significant judgment is required in evaluating and estimating our provision and accruals for these taxes. Our income tax liabilities are dependent upon the location of earnings among these different jurisdictions. Our income tax provision and income tax liabilities could be adversely affected by the jurisdictional mix of earnings, changes in valuation of deferred tax assets and liabilities and changes in tax treaties, laws and regulations.

The Company is currently a party in various litigation matters and tax and environmental proceedings and faces risks arising from various unasserted litigation matters, including product liability, patent infringement, antitrust claims, and claims for third-party property damage or personal injury stemming from alleged torts, including, as discussed elsewhere in this Report, a number of cases seeking damages for alleged exposure to asbestos-contaminated talc products sold by BMI Oldco. Any failure to appropriately manage safety, human health, product liability and environmental risks associated with the Company’s products and production processes could adversely impact the Company’s employees and other stakeholders, the Company’s reputation, and its results of operations, cash flows and financial condition. Public perception of the risks associated with the Company’s products and production processes could impact product acceptance and influence the regulatory environment in which the Company operates. Any unanticipated liability arising out of a current matter or proceeding, or from the other risks described above, could have a material adverse effect on the Company’s results of operations, cash flows and financial condition.

Production facilities are subject to operating risks and capacity limitations that may adversely affect the Company’s financial condition or results of operations.

The Company is dependent on the continued operation of its production facilities. Production facilities are subject to hazards associated with the manufacturing, handling, storage, and transportation of chemical materials and products, including pipeline leaks and ruptures, explosions, fires, inclement weather and natural disasters, mechanical failure, unscheduled downtime, labor difficulties, transportation interruptions, and environmental risks. Production facilities are also subject to governmental requirements that may, and during the Covid-19 pandemic did, affect our ability to operate. We maintain property, business interruption and casualty insurance but such insurance may not cover all risks associated with the hazards of our business and is subject to limitations, including deductibles and maximum liabilities covered. We may incur losses beyond the limits, or outside the coverage, of our insurance policies. Further, from time to time, we may experience capacity limitations in our manufacturing operations. In addition, if we are unable to effectively forecast our customers’ demand, it could affect our ability to successfully manage operating capacity limitations. These hazards, limitations, disruptions in supply and capacity constraints could adversely affect financial results.

target_risks.name: Climate-related legislation and regulation restricting greenhouse gas emissions
target_risks.description: Climate-related legislation or regulation restricting greenhouse gas emissions in regions where the Company operates could adversely affect operations or product demand.
target_risks.why: The Company's manufacturing uses significant energy, and increased energy prices from such legislation may not be passable to customers, potentially reducing profitability and demand for products.

peer_risks.name: Limited operating history and no revenue
peer_risks.description: The company has no customers, no revenue, and a very limited operating history, making it difficult to evaluate its business or predict future performance.
peer_risks.why: Global Gas Corp currently has no customers and has not generated any revenue, and investors cannot base assumptions on its operating history or future prospects.

peer_risks.name: Failure to secure customers or execute contracts
peer_risks.description: The company may fail to negotiate, sign, or successfully execute contracts with customers and suppliers, which is critical to its business model.
peer_risks.why: The company cannot assure it will successfully negotiate contracts or execute them if signed, and its entire business strategy depends on securing and delivering on these contracts.

peer_risks.name: Unproven business model
peer_risks.description: The company's business model has yet to be tested, and failure to commercialize its plans could harm its reputation and lead to liabilities exceeding its resources.
peer_risks.why: The business model is untested, and any failure to commercialize strategic plans could result in substantial liabilities that exceed the company’s resources.

peer_risks.name: Project delays and cost overruns
peer_risks.description: Engineering, procurement, and construction projects may face delays and cost overruns due to factors beyond the company’s control.
peer_risks.why: Delays from regulatory permits, labor shortages, weather, supplier issues, customer scope changes, and equipment delivery can cause substantial delays and costs, potentially requiring project cancellation or customer compensation.

peer_risks.name: Financing risks for large projects
peer_risks.description: The company may face difficulties securing financing for large projects, with terms that could trigger default if performance requirements are not met.
peer_risks.why: Financing arrangements for large projects may require performance compliance; failure to meet these could result in default, restructuring costs, or other losses.

peer_risks.name: Operational hazards at facilities
peer_risks.description: Operations involve hazards like pipeline leaks, fires, explosions, and cyber incidents that could cause loss of life, environmental damage, or production loss.
peer_risks.why: The company’s facilities inherently entail hazards such as leaks, explosions, and cyber incidents, which could negatively impact operations, reputation, and cash flows.

peer_risks.name: Inadequate management experience for public company
peer_risks.description: Management has limited experience running a publicly traded company and may fail to meet regulatory and reporting obligations.
peer_risks.why: Management lacks experience with public company regulations, potentially impairing timely SEC filings, Sarbanes-Oxley compliance, and internal controls, requiring costly system upgrades.

peer_risks.name: Inability to manage growth
peer_risks.description: Rapid growth could overwhelm the company’s financial, technical, and management resources, hindering execution of its business plan.
peer_risks.why: Growth will strain limited resources, and failure to upgrade control systems or handle unexpected expansion could materially affect operations and business plan execution.

peer_risks.name: Volatility in energy costs
peer_risks.description: Fluctuations in energy prices due to geopolitical conflicts could increase operating and shipping costs for potential facilities and projects.
peer_risks.why: The Russia-Ukraine conflict and Middle East hostilities have increased energy prices, raising costs for manufacturing, material shipping, and natural gas procurement for projects.

peer_risks.name: Reliance on third-party suppliers and subcontractors
peer_risks.description: Dependence on third parties for equipment and services exposes the company to their failures, interruptions, or quality issues.
peer_risks.why: Supplier or subcontractor failures—including labor disputes, credit access issues, or poor performance—could interrupt supply, cause customer dissatisfaction, or prevent delivery to customers.

peer_risks.name: Losses on fixed-price contracts
peer_risks.description: Fixed-price contracts may lead to losses if cost overruns, delays, or defects exceed profit margins or trigger penalties.
peer_risks.why: Contracts include penalties or liquidated damages for delays or defects, and cost overruns may erode or eliminate expected profits, potentially resulting in project losses.

peer_risks.name: Catastrophic events or natural disasters
peer_risks.description: Extreme weather, pandemics, war, or terrorism could impair production, distribution, and supply chains, and expose the company to third-party liability.
peer_risks.why: Such events could disrupt operations, cause customer/supplier outages, and limit supply of energy and raw materials needed for normal business operations.

peer_risks.name: Inability to attract, hire, and retain qualified personnel
peer_risks.description: Failure to secure or retain skilled employees could hinder product development, marketing, sales, and overall business management.
peer_risks.why: The company depends on a highly skilled, experienced, and efficient workforce; loss of key employees in skilled areas could negatively affect financial results.

peer_risks.name: Uncertainty in completing hydrogen production projects
peer_risks.description: Construction and operation of hydrogen production facilities may be delayed, exceed budget, or fail to meet customer demand.
peer_risks.why: Timing and costs are subject to factors outside the company's control, and projects may take longer or cost more than expected to become operational.

peer_risks.name: Unfavorable laws, regulations, and policies for hydrogen production
peer_risks.description: Hydrogen projects may be hindered by nascent, inconsistent, or unfavorable regulatory frameworks across jurisdictions.
peer_risks.why: Laws and policies are evolving and vary by region; there is no guarantee they will support the company’s projects, and new permitting requirements may apply.

peer_risks.name: Intense competition in hydrogen production
peer_risks.description: Hydrogen facilities face robust competition from well-established multinational energy companies.
peer_risks.why: The competitive environment may prevent the company’s hydrogen strategy from succeeding, even if projects are completed on time and budget.

peer_risks.name: Risks from joint ventures
peer_risks.description: Joint ventures may involve misaligned goals, partner failure to meet obligations, or lack of control over operations and systems.
peer_risks.why: The company may have limited ability to direct management, accounting, IT, or governance systems of joint ventures, exposing it to liability and reputational damage.

peer_risks.name: Inadequate protection of proprietary intellectual property
peer_risks.description: Failure to secure or defend patents and proprietary technology could lead to competitive harm.
peer_risks.why: Patent applications may not be granted, protection may be insufficient, and defending IP could require significant resources without guaranteed success.

peer_risks.name: Economic downturn and inflation
peer_risks.description: Economic weakness, inflation, and higher interest rates may reduce customer demand and spending on the company’s products and services.
peer_risks.why: Customers may reduce capital spending, face credit constraints, or experience supply chain disruptions, leading to lower customer acquisition and revenue.

peer_risks.name: Government regulation and compliance costs
peer_risks.description: Compliance with complex and changing regulations on taxes, anti-bribery, export controls, and other areas may increase costs or reduce profitability.
peer_risks.why: Non-compliance could lead to penalties, sanctions, reputational damage, and legal fees; export restrictions may block market access or raise shipping costs.

peer_risks.name: Liability for employee or partner misconduct
peer_risks.description: Improper actions by employees, agents, or acquired businesses could expose the company to legal and reputational risks.
peer_risks.why: The company may be held liable for violations of anti-bribery, fraud, data privacy, or export laws committed by others, even if not directly involved.

peer_risks.name: Environmental regulations and contamination liability
peer_risks.description: Environmental laws may require costly compliance, cleanup, or result in liability for contamination at owned or operated sites.
peer_risks.why: Laws like CERCLA impose strict liability for remediation costs without regard to fault, and violations can lead to fines, penalties, or operational shutdowns.

peer_risks.name: Delays in obtaining permits for production facilities
peer_risks.description: Unexpected delays in securing required permits could hinder the operation of hydrogen production facilities.
peer_risks.why: Permitting processes may require significant time and financial resources, delaying operations and negatively impacting business prospects and financial results.

peer_risks.name: Ineffective greenhouse gas capture technologies
peer_risks.description: GHG capture technologies may not fully capture emissions, increasing exposure to regulatory and cost pressures related to climate change.
peer_risks.why: If technologies fail to capture 100% of GHGs, new regulations or public pressure could raise costs for power, hydrogen production, or gasification processes.

peer_risks.name: Evolving ESG standards and regulations
peer_risks.description: Evolving ESG laws, regulations, and standards globally may cause our practices to fall short of investor or stakeholder expectations, harming reputation and attractiveness as a business partner or employer.
peer_risks.why: New ESG frameworks and disclosure requirements are being formalized in Europe, the U.S., Asia, and elsewhere, and failure to meet them could negatively impact our reputation and investment appeal.

peer_risks.name: Compliance with environmental and safety regulations
peer_risks.description: Extensive federal, state, local, and foreign environmental and safety laws may require significant unforeseen expenditures for equipment, compliance, and remediation, adversely affecting financial results.
peer_risks.why: Operations involve emissions, hazardous waste, and transportation risks, and future stricter regulations may force costly upgrades or remediation not currently anticipated.

peer_risks.name: Regulation of chemicals and materials in products
peer_risks.description: Increasing government restrictions on chemicals and materials in product components may require costly compliance efforts and alter product design or sourcing.
peer_risks.why: Laws or policies may target substances within our product components, obligating us to modify formulations or sourcing to meet new requirements.

peer_risks.name: New regulations on hydrogen and other products
peer_risks.description: Future regulations on hydrogen production, distribution, installation, or servicing could increase costs, reduce demand, or subject us to penalties for noncompliance.
peer_risks.why: Governments may impose new rules on hydrogen and related products at any level, potentially leading to fines, injunctions, or higher prices that reduce competitiveness.

peer_risks.name: Supply chain disruptions for raw materials and energy
peer_risks.description: Disruptions in supply of energy, biogas, renewable natural gas, or other raw materials could prevent fulfillment of contracts and harm financial results.
peer_risks.why: Supply may be interrupted by market conditions, regulatory actions, natural events, pandemics, or transportation delays, including those from COVID-19 resurgences.

peer_risks.name: Inability to pass through rising energy and raw material costs
peer_risks.description: Rising energy and raw material costs may not be fully recoverable from customers due to competitive pressures, leading to reduced margins and lower earnings.
peer_risks.why: Cost pass-throughs may result in declining margins, and competitive pressures may prevent price increases, causing revenue and earnings to suffer.

peer_risks.name: Supply shortages of necessary parts and raw materials
peer_risks.description: Inability to source critical parts or raw materials due to regulatory, logistical, or geopolitical factors could disrupt operations or cause delays.
peer_risks.why: Supplies may be reduced by regulatory requirements, supplier financial distress, tariffs, transportation issues, pandemics, severe weather, or conflicts.

peer_risks.name: Product safety and liability risks from hydrogen and gases
peer_risks.description: Production, transport, or storage of inherently dangerous gases like hydrogen may lead to liability claims, recalls, or reputational damage reducing demand.
peer_risks.why: Malfunctions, accidents, or perceived safety issues could trigger product liability claims, negative publicity, or regulatory scrutiny, harming demand and financial prospects.

peer_risks.name: Operational risks from complex machinery and plant failures
peer_risks.description: Unexpected malfunctions in large-scale gas generation and carbon recovery plants may cause production delays, safety incidents, environmental damage, or legal liabilities.
peer_risks.why: Plant components depend on repairs and spare parts that may be unavailable, and failures can result from environmental hazards, labor disputes, natural disasters, or system defects.

peer_risks.name: Competition from larger and smaller rivals
peer_risks.description: Competition from larger firms with greater resources or smaller regional players may weaken demand, lower pricing, or reduce our market share.
peer_risks.why: Competitors may introduce new technologies or expand capacity faster, and established firms may enter our market, impacting profitability and competitiveness.

peer_risks.name: Cybersecurity breaches and IT system failures
peer_risks.description: Cyberattacks or IT system failures may compromise confidential data, leading to legal exposure, financial loss, and reputational damage.
peer_risks.why: Systems may be breached by malicious actors or insiders, or disrupted by natural disasters or failures, exposing proprietary and personal data with insufficient insurance coverage.

peer_risks.name: Reliance on third-party vendors with access to confidential data
peer_risks.description: Outsourcing operations to third parties increases exposure to data breaches, with limited recourse if their systems are compromised.
peer_risks.why: Vendors have access to confidential information, and if their systems are breached, we may lack sufficient legal recourse and must spend resources to mitigate the impact.

peer_risks.name: Estimates and assumptions in financial reporting
peer_risks.description: Accounting estimates used in preparing financial statements may differ from actual results, materially impacting financial condition and results of operations.
peer_risks.why: Financial statements rely on assumptions about assets, liabilities, revenues, and expenses based on available data, and actual outcomes may vary significantly from these estimates.

peer_risks.name: Tax law changes may adversely affect profitability
peer_risks.description: New or changed U.S. tax laws, rates, or interpretations could reduce after-tax income and harm business and financial results.
peer_risks.why: Increases in income tax rates or adverse changes in tax laws in jurisdictions where Holdings operates can directly reduce after-tax income, and existing laws are subject to future modification or application.

{"source_page": 14, "section_title": "Item 1A.  Risk Factors", "source_text": "The Company operates in very competitive industries, which could adversely affect our profitability.

The Company has many competitors. Some of our principal competitors have greater financial and other resources than we have. Accordingly, these competitors may be better able to withstand economic downturns and changes in conditions within the industries in which we operate and may have significantly greater operating and financial flexibility than we do. We also face competition for some of our products from alternative products, and some of the competition we face comes from competitors in lower-cost production countries like China and India. As a result of the competitive environment in the markets in which we operate, we currently face and will continue to face pressure on the sales prices of our products from competitors, which could reduce profit margins.

The Company’s sales could be adversely affected by consolidation in customer industries.

Several consolidations in the paper industry have taken place in recent years and such consolidation could continue in the future. These consolidations could result in partial or total closure of some paper mills where the Company operates satellite plants. Such closures would reduce the Company’s sales, except to the extent that they resulted in shifting paper production and associated purchases of calcium carbonate to another location served by the Company. Similarly, consolidations have occurred in the foundry and steel industries. Such consolidations in the major industries we serve concentrate purchasing power in the hands of a smaller number of manufacturers, enabling them to increase pressure on suppliers, such as the Company. This increased pressure could have an adverse effect on the Company’s results of operations in the future.

The Company’s sales could be adversely affected by our failure to renew or extend long-term sales contracts for our satellite operations.

The Company’s sales of calcium carbonate to paper customers are typically pursuant to long-term evergreen agreements, initially ten years in length, with paper mills where the Company operates satellite plants. Sales pursuant to these contracts represent a significant portion of our sales in the Specialty Additives product line of the Consumer & Specialties segment. The terms of many of these agreements have been extended or renewed in the past, often in connection with an expansion of the satellite plant. However, failure of a number of the Company’s customers to renew or extend existing agreements on terms as favorable to the Company as those currently in effect, or at all, could have a substantial adverse effect on the Company’s results of operations, and could also result in impairment of the assets associated with the satellite plant.

Financial Risks

Servicing the Company’s debt will require a significant amount of cash. This could reduce the Company’s flexibility to respond to changing business and economic conditions or fund capital expenditures or working capital needs. Our ability to generate cash depends on many factors beyond our control.

At December 31, 2024, the Company had $971.3 million aggregate principal amount of total indebtedness (consisting primarily of $575.0 million aggregate principal amount of loans under our term facility, $400.0 million aggregate principal amount of notes and $4.5 million outstanding under our revolving credit facility) and an additional $386.4 million of borrowing capacity under the revolving credit facility (after giving effect to $9.1 million of outstanding letters of credit). Our outstanding indebtedness will require a significant amount of cash to make interest payments. Further, the interest rate on a significant portion of our borrowings under our senior secured credit facility is based on SOFR interest rates, which has resulted in and could continue to result in higher interest expense in the event of continued increases in interest rates. Our ability to pay interest on our debt and to satisfy our other debt obligations will depend in part upon our future financial and operating performance and upon our ability to renew or refinance borrowings. Prevailing economic conditions and financial, business, competitive, regulatory and other factors, many of which are beyond our control, will affect our ability to make these payments. We cannot guarantee that our business will generate sufficient cash flow from operations or that future borrowings will be available to us in an amount sufficient to enable us to fund our liquidity needs. If we are unable to generate sufficient cash flow to meet our debt service obligations, we will have to pursue one or more alternatives, such as reducing or delaying capital or other expenditures, refinancing debt, selling assets, or raising equity capital. Further, the requirement to make significant interest payments may reduce the Company’s flexibility to respond to changing business and economic conditions or fund capital expenditure or working capital needs and may increase the Company’s vulnerability to adverse economic conditions.

The agreement governing our senior secured credit facility and the indenture that governs our 5.0% Senior Notes due 2028 contain a number of significant covenants that, among other things, limit our ability to: incur or guarantee additional indebtedness, pay dividends or make other distributions or repurchase or redeem capital stock, prepay, redeem or repurchase certain debt, issue certain preferred stock or similar equity securities, make loans and investments, sell or otherwise dispose of assets, incur liens, enter into transactions with affiliates, enter into agreements restricting our subsidiaries’ ability to pay dividends and consolidate, merge or sell all or substantially all of our assets. In addition, we are required to comply with specific financial ratios, including a maximum net leverage ratio, under which we are required to achieve specific financial results. Our ability to comply with these provisions may be affected by events beyond our control. A breach of any of these covenants would result in a default under the applicable agreements. In the event of any default under our senior secured credit facility, our lenders could elect to declare all amounts borrowed under the credit agreement, together with accrued interest thereon, to be due and payable. In such an event, we cannot assure you that we would have sufficient assets to pay debt then outstanding under the credit agreement, the indenture governing our notes, and any other agreements governing our debt. Any future refinancing of the senior secured credit facility is likely to contain similar restrictive covenants. We may also incur future debt obligations that might subject us to additional restrictive covenants that could affect our financial and operational flexibility. We cannot assure you that we will be granted waivers or amendments to these agreements if for any reason we are unable to comply with these agreements or that we will be able to refinance our debt on terms acceptable to us, or at all.

Technology, Development and Growth Risks

The Company’s results could be adversely affected if it is unable to effectively achieve and implement its growth initiatives.

Sales and income growth of the Company depends upon a number of uncertain events. Growth will depend in part on sales growth from our existing businesses and customers. The Company has a strategic growth initiative to increase penetration into geographic markets such as Brazil, India and China as well as other Asian and Eastern European countries. The Company also has a strategic growth initiative to increase penetration into consumer-oriented markets such as pet litter, personal care, and oil purification. Our strategy also anticipates growth through future acquisitions. However, our ability to identify and consummate any future acquisitions on terms that are favorable to us may be limited by the number of attractive acquisition targets, internal demands on our resources and our ability to obtain financing. Our success in integrating newly acquired businesses will depend upon our ability to retain key personnel, avoid diversion of management’s attention from operational matters, and integrate general and administrative services. In addition, future acquisitions could result in the incurrence of additional debt, costs and contingent liabilities. Integration of acquired operations may take longer, or be more costly or disruptive to our business, than originally anticipated, and it is also possible that expected synergies from future acquisitions may not materialize. We also may incur costs and divert management attention with regard to potential acquisitions that are never consummated. Difficulties, delays or failure of any of these strategies could affect the future growth rate of the Company.

Delays or failures in new product development could adversely affect the Company’s operations.

The Company’s future business success will depend in part upon its ability to maintain and enhance its technological capabilities, to respond to changing customer needs, and to successfully anticipate or respond to technological changes on a cost-effective and timely basis. The Company is engaged in a continuous effort to develop new products and processes in all of its product lines. Difficulties, delays or failures in the development, testing, production, marketing or sale of such new products could cause actual results of operations to differ materially from our expected results.

The Company’s ability to compete is dependent upon its ability to defend its intellectual property against inappropriate disclosure, theft and infringement.

The Company’s ability to compete is based in part upon proprietary knowledge, both patented and unpatented. The Company’s ability to achieve anticipated results depends in part on its ability to defend its intellectual property against inappropriate disclosure and theft as well as against infringement. In addition, development by the Company’s competitors of new products or technologies that are more effective or less expensive than those the Company offers could have a material adverse effect on the Company’s financial condition or results of operations.

{"source_page": 17, "section_title": "Item 1A.  Risk Factors", "source_text": "The Company relies on shipping bulk cargos of bentonite from the United States, Turkey and China to customers, as well as our own subsidiaries, and we are sensitive to our ability to recover these shipping costs. If we cannot secure our container requirements or offset additional shipping costs with price increases to customers, our profitability could be impacted. We are also subject to other shipping risks. In particular, rail service interruptions have affected our ability to ship, and the availability of rail service, and our ability to recover increased rail costs, may be beyond our control. In addition, governmental restrictions can, and during the COVID-19 pandemic did, affect our ability to ship our products.

Operational Risks

The Company’s subsidiaries, BMI Oldco Inc. (f/k/a Barretts Minerals Inc.) (“Oldco”) and Barretts Ventures Texas LLC (together with Oldco, the “Chapter 11 Debtors”), have filed voluntary petitions for relief under Chapter 11 of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code to address and comprehensively resolve Oldco’s liabilities associated with talc. Risks and uncertainties related to this filing could have a material adverse effect on the Company’s business, financial condition, results of operations and cash flows.

The Company and certain of the Company’s subsidiaries are among numerous defendants in over six hundred cases seeking damages for alleged exposure to asbestos-contaminated talc products sold by the Company’s subsidiary Oldco. On October 2, 2023 (the “Petition Date”), notwithstanding the Company’s confidence in the safety of Oldco’s talc products, the Chapter 11 Debtors filed voluntary petitions for relief under Chapter 11 of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Texas (the “Chapter 11 Cases”) to address and comprehensively resolve Oldco’s liabilities associated with talc. Minerals Technologies Inc. and the Company’s other subsidiaries were not included in the Chapter 11 filing. In the second quarter of 2024, Oldco sold its talc assets under section 363 of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code.

In addition, in the second quarter of 2024, the Company entered into a Debtor-in-Possession Credit Agreement with Oldco (the "DIP Credit Agreement") and recorded a provision for credit loss of $30 million for the maximum aggregate principal amount under such DIP Credit Agreement.

Proceeds of the sale of Oldco's talc assets and funds drawn by Oldco under the DIP Credit Agreement will be used to fund the Chapter 11 Cases. The Chapter 11 Debtors' ultimate goal in the Chapter 11 Cases is to confirm a plan of reorganization under Section 524(g) of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code and utilize this provision of the Bankruptcy Code to establish a trust that will address all current and future talc-related claims. In January 2024, the Chapter 11 Debtors and Minerals Technologies Inc. commenced a court-approved mediation process with the Official Committee of Unsecured Creditors (appointed in the Chapter 11 Cases as the representative of current talc claimants)

(the “Committee”)

and the Future Claimants Representative (appointed in the Chapter 11 Cases as the representative of future talc claimants) regarding the terms of a potential consensual plan of reorganization and the ultimate amount to be contributed to any trust. The mediation process is ongoing. During the pendency of the Chapter 11 Cases, the Company anticipates that the Chapter 11 Debtors will benefit from the operation of the automatic stay, which stays ongoing litigation in connection with talc-related claims against the Chapter 11 Debtors. In addition, subject to certain exceptions, the filing or continued prosecution of all talc-related claims against the Chapter 11 Debtors' non-debtor affiliates is temporarily stayed through April 15, 2025 (subject to further extensions), the date on which a hearing is scheduled on the status of the Chapter 11 Cases. The Chapter 11 Debtors have been deconsolidated from the Company’s financial statements since the Petition Date.

Although the Chapter 11 Cases are progressing, it is not possible at this time to predict how the Bankruptcy Court will rule on the Committee’s motion to dismiss the Chapter 11 Cases, the form of any ultimate resolution or when an ultimate resolution might occur. Accordingly, the amount that will be necessary to fully and finally resolve all of Oldco’s current and future talc-related claims in connection with a confirmed Chapter 11 plan of reorganization cannot be estimated at this time. Several risks and uncertainties related to the Chapter 11 Cases could have a material adverse effect on the Company’s business, financial condition, results of operations and cash flows, including the ultimate amount necessary to be contributed to any trust established pursuant to Section 524(g) of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code, the potential for the Company’s talc-related exposure to extend beyond

the Chapter 11 Debtors

arising from claims by talc plaintiffs relating to the Company’s liability for talc claims, corporate veil piercing efforts or otherwise, any final resolution of the scope of the Pfizer indemnity, the ongoing costs of the Chapter 11 Cases, which may require additional funding from time to time, the cost and the length of time necessary to ultimately resolve the cases, either through settlement or as a result of litigation arising in connection with the Chapter 11 Cases, and the possibility that the Chapter 11 Debtors will be unsuccessful in attaining relief under Chapter 11. Further, while the Company anticipates that

the Chapter 11 Debtors

will benefit from the operation of the automatic stay during the Chapter 11 proceedings, depending on the ultimate outcome of any of these litigation matters, the Company could in the future be required to pay significant amounts as a result of settlements or judgments, potentially in excess of liabilities accrued to date in respect of such matters. The resolution of, or recognition of additional liabilities in connection with, pending or future litigation could have a material adverse effect on the Company’s results of operations, cash flows and financial condition.

For a further discussion of the Chapter 11 Cases and Oldco's talc-related liabilities, see Note 17 to the Consolidated Financial Statements, included in this report.

{"source_page": 18, "section_title": "Item 1A.  Risk Factors", "source_text": "The Company is subject to stringent regulation in the areas of environmental, health and safety, and tax, and may incur unanticipated costs or liabilities arising out of claims for various legal, environmental and tax matters or product stewardship issues that could materially harm the Company’s results of operations, cash flows and financial condition.

The Company’s operations are subject to international, federal, state and local governmental environmental, health and safety, tax and other laws and regulations. We have expended, and may be required to expend in the future, substantial funds for compliance with such laws and regulations. In addition, future events, such as changes to or modifications of interpretations of existing laws and regulations, or enforcement polices, or further investigation or evaluation of the potential environmental impacts of operations or health hazards of certain products, may affect our mining rights or give rise to additional compliance and other costs that could have a material adverse effect on the Company. Further, certain of our customers are subject to various federal and international laws and regulations relating to environmental and health and safety matters, especially customers of our Environmental & Infrastructure product line of our Engineered Solutions segment, who are subject to drilling permits, waste water disposal and other regulations. To the extent that these laws and regulations affecting our customers change, demand for our products and services could also change and thereby affect our financial results. State, national, and international governments and agencies have been evaluating climate-related legislation and regulation that would restrict emissions of greenhouse gases in areas in which we conduct business, and some such legislation and regulation have already been enacted or adopted. Enactment of climate-related legislation or adoption of regulation that restrict emissions of greenhouse gases in areas in which we conduct business could have an adverse effect on our operations or demand for our products. Our manufacturing processes for our products use a significant amount of energy and, should energy prices increase as a result of such legislation or regulation, we may not be able to pass these increased costs on to purchasers of our products. We cannot predict if or when currently proposed or additional laws and regulations regarding climate change or other environmental or health and safety concerns will be enacted or adopted.

The Company is also subject to income tax laws and regulations in the United States and various foreign jurisdictions. Significant judgment is required in evaluating and estimating our provision and accruals for these taxes. Our income tax liabilities are dependent upon the location of earnings among these different jurisdictions. Our income tax provision and income tax liabilities could be adversely affected by the jurisdictional mix of earnings, changes in valuation of deferred tax assets and liabilities and changes in tax treaties, laws and regulations.

The Company is currently a party in various litigation matters and tax and environmental proceedings and faces risks arising from various unasserted litigation matters, including product liability, patent infringement, antitrust claims, and claims for third-party property damage or personal injury stemming from alleged torts, including, as discussed elsewhere in this Report, a number of cases seeking damages for alleged exposure to asbestos-contaminated talc products sold by BMI Oldco. Any failure to appropriately manage safety, human health, product liability and environmental risks associated with the Company’s products and production processes could adversely impact the Company’s employees and other stakeholders, the Company’s reputation, and its results of operations, cash flows and financial condition. Public perception of the risks associated with the Company’s products and production processes could impact product acceptance and influence the regulatory environment in which the Company operates. Any unanticipated liability arising out of a current matter or proceeding, or from the other risks described above, could have a material adverse effect on the Company’s results of operations, cash flows and financial condition.

Production facilities are subject to operating risks and capacity limitations that may adversely affect the Company’s financial condition or results of operations.

The Company is dependent on the continued operation of its production facilities. Production facilities are subject to hazards associated with the manufacturing, handling, storage, and transportation of chemical materials and products, including pipeline leaks and ruptures, explosions, fires, inclement weather and natural disasters, mechanical failure, unscheduled downtime, labor difficulties, transportation interruptions, and environmental risks. Production facilities are also subject to governmental requirements that may, and during the Covid-19 pandemic did, affect our ability to operate. We maintain property, business interruption and casualty insurance but such insurance may not cover all risks associated with the hazards of our business and is subject to limitations, including deductibles and maximum liabilities covered. We may incur losses beyond the limits, or outside the coverage, of our insurance policies. Further, from time to time, we may experience capacity limitations in our manufacturing operations. In addition, if we are unable to effectively forecast our customers’ demand, it could affect our ability to successfully manage operating capacity limitations. These hazards, limitations, disruptions in supply and capacity constraints could adversely affect financial results.

target_risks.name: Climate-related legislation and regulation restricting greenhouse gas emissions
target_risks.description: Climate-related legislation or regulation restricting greenhouse gas emissions in regions where the Company operates could adversely affect operations or product demand.
target_risks.why: The Company's manufacturing uses significant energy, and increased energy prices from such legislation may not be passable to customers, potentially reducing profitability and demand for products.

peer_risks.name: Demand for and prices of TiO2 products are influenced by changing market conditions
peer_risks.description: TiO2 demand and pricing are tied to global economic conditions and discretionary spending, which can reduce earnings or cause operating losses.
peer_risks.why: In 2023, 90% of the Chemicals Segment’s sales were TiO2, and demand historically correlates with GDP and discretionary spending, which can decline due to regional or global events.

peer_risks.name: Cyclical pricing in the global TiO2 industry affects profitability
peer_risks.description: TiO2 pricing is cyclical and sensitive to global economic conditions, directly impacting selling prices, profit margins, and cash flows.
peer_risks.why: Historically, TiO2 markets alternate between periods of increasing and decreasing demand, with selling prices and margins rising or falling accordingly.

peer_risks.name: Customer inventory behavior driven by anticipated price changes
peer_risks.description: Customers may accelerate or defer TiO2 purchases based on anticipated price movements, disrupting sales volume and revenue predictability.
peer_risks.why: Customers may buy ahead of expected price increases or delay purchases ahead of anticipated price decreases, affecting timing and volume of sales.

peer_risks.name: Limited capacity expansion without additional investment
peer_risks.description: Inability to increase TiO2 production capacity without costly greenfield or brownfield investments heightens reliance on pricing for profitability.
peer_risks.why: The Chemicals Segment’s ability to expand capacity without new investment is limited, making profitability more dependent on product selling prices.

peer_risks.name: Intense competition in the concentrated TiO2 industry
peer_risks.description: The TiO2 industry is concentrated and highly competitive, with price pressures from global competitors reducing earnings.
peer_risks.why: Top five producers control 52% of global capacity, and competitors—including Chinese producers with lower costs—can drive down prices.

peer_risks.name: Competitive threat from Chinese TiO2 producers using chloride technology
peer_risks.description: Chinese producers developing chloride process technology may substitute VALHI’s products, increasing competitive pressure.
peer_risks.why: Chinese producers are advancing chloride technology and improving sulfate/chloride product quality, raising risk of substitution.

peer_risks.name: Competitors with lower costs or vertical integration gain pricing advantage
peer_risks.description: Competitors with lower costs or vertically integrated raw materials can undercut VALHI’s prices, especially during raw material spikes.
peer_risks.why: Some competitors have vertically integrated raw material sources or operate under less stringent regulations, giving them cost advantages.

peer_risks.name: Competitors with greater resources respond faster to market changes
peer_risks.description: Larger competitors with more financial and technological resources may outpace VALHI in adapting to technology and customer needs.
peer_risks.why: Some competitors have greater resources and can respond more quickly to emerging technologies and customer requirements.

peer_risks.name: Consolidation among competitors or customers reduces demand or competitiveness
peer_risks.description: Consolidation among competitors or customers may reduce demand for VALHI’s products or strengthen competitors’ market position.
peer_risks.why: Consolidation could lead to reduced demand or make it harder to compete against larger, consolidated entities.

peer_risks.name: Pricing pressure in mature Component Products markets
peer_risks.description: Mature, highly competitive markets for Component Products lead to pricing pressure and cost-reduction demands.
peer_risks.why: Many markets served are mature and competitive, with numerous competitors offering similar products, forcing pricing discipline.

peer_risks.name: Competitors sourcing lower-cost products from Asia undercut pricing
peer_risks.description: Competitors sourcing products from Asia can drive prices below VALHI’s ability to adjust costs, reducing margins.
peer_risks.why: Competitors can lower prices beyond VALHI’s cost-adjustment capacity, especially due to lower production costs in Asia.

peer_risks.name: Competitors with greater resources withstand market changes better
peer_risks.description: Competitors with superior financial and technological resources may outlast VALHI during market downturns.
peer_risks.why: Some competitors have greater financial, technological, and other resources, enabling them to better withstand market volatility.

peer_risks.name: Competitors respond faster to new technologies and customer requirements
peer_risks.description: Competitors may adapt more quickly than VALHI to technological changes and evolving customer demands.
peer_risks.why: Competitors may respond more rapidly to new technologies and customer requirements, reducing VALHI’s competitive edge.

peer_risks.name: Loss of market share with key customers reduces demand
peer_risks.description: Reduced market share with key customers or their end-product customers lowers demand for VALHI’s Component Products.
peer_risks.why: A reduction in VALHI’s market share with key customers—or their customers’ market share—can directly reduce product demand.

peer_risks.name: New competitors can emerge by modifying existing facilities
peer_risks.description: Existing manufacturers can retool to produce competing products, increasing market competition unexpectedly.
peer_risks.why: New competitors may emerge by modifying existing production facilities to manufacture products that compete with VALHI’s.

peer_risks.name: Inability to sustain competitive cost structure
peer_risks.description: VALHI may fail to maintain a cost structure that allows it to compete effectively in its markets.
peer_risks.why: The Component Products Segment may not be able to sustain a cost structure enabling competitiveness against lower-cost rivals.

peer_risks.name: Customers may prioritize lower-cost products over quality
peer_risks.description: Customers may stop valuing VALHI’s product design, quality, or durability in favor of cheaper alternatives.
peer_risks.why: Customers may no longer value VALHI’s product design, quality, or durability over lower-cost competitors’ products.

peer_risks.name: Failure of new product innovations to achieve commercial success
peer_risks.description: New product features may not achieve the same success as existing products, risking lost development investment.
peer_risks.why: There is no guarantee that new product features will achieve the same degree of success as existing products, and development costs may not be recoverable.

peer_risks.name: Unrecoverable development costs if customers abandon custom innovations
peer_risks.description: VALHI may bear full development costs for custom innovations that customers later reject or abandon.
peer_risks.why: If a customer rejects or abandons custom product innovation efforts, VALHI may not recover its development costs.

peer_risks.name: Higher costs or limited availability of TiO2 feedstock reduces earnings and liquidity
peer_risks.description: Raw material shortages or price increases for titanium feedstock can reduce margins and liquidity.
peer_risks.why: Feedstock is sourced from limited global suppliers; price increases in 2022–2023 affected margins, and supply disruptions could force production cuts.

peer_risks.name: Political or regulatory instability in raw material supply countries
peer_risks.description: Political or regulatory instability in feedstock-supplying countries may disrupt raw material availability.
peer_risks.why: Political and economic instability or increased regulations in countries supplying titanium feedstock could adversely affect availability.

peer_risks.name: Failure to renew long-term feedstock supply contracts
peer_risks.description: Inability to renew or extend long-term feedstock contracts may disrupt supply or increase costs.
peer_risks.why: VALHI has minimum purchase commitments of $583M from 2024–2026 and cannot guarantee renewal of these contracts upon expiration.

peer_risks.name: Fixed minimum purchase commitments create financial risk if production declines
peer_risks.description: Mandatory minimum feedstock purchases may become a financial burden if production is reduced.
peer_risks.why: If production is significantly reduced, VALHI may be unable to modify contractual commitments for $583M in feedstock purchases through 2026.

peer_risks.name: Inadequate protection of trade secrets and proprietary know-how
peer_risks.description: Confidentiality agreements may not sufficiently protect trade secrets or provide adequate remedies for breaches, and breaches may not be readily detectable.
peer_risks.why: The company acknowledges that confidentiality agreements with employees and third parties may not provide sufficient protection or available remedies for unauthorized use or disclosure of proprietary expertise, and breaches may go undetected.

peer_risks.name: Intellectual property rights being challenged, invalidated, or misappropriated
peer_risks.description: Patents, trademarks, and trade secrets may be challenged, circumvented, or misappropriated by third parties, including through independent discovery.
peer_risks.why: Despite legal protections, intellectual property rights could be challenged, invalidated, circumvented, or misappropriated, and third parties may independently discover trade secrets, rendering enforcement impossible.

peer_risks.name: Uncertainty in approval of pending trademark and patent applications
peer_risks.description: There is no guarantee that pending trademark or patent applications for the Component Products Segment will be approved.
peer_risks.why: The company explicitly states it does not know if any of its pending trademark or patent applications will be approved, creating uncertainty in securing legal protection.

peer_risks.name: Intellectual property infringement claims by third parties
peer_risks.description: Third parties may claim the company or its customers infringe their intellectual property, leading to costly litigation or forced licensing.
peer_risks.why: Even meritless claims can be time-consuming and costly to defend, and may require redesigning technology, entering costly settlements, paying damages, or facing injunctions against selling products.

peer_risks.name: High cost and uncertainty of litigation to enforce intellectual property rights
peer_risks.description: Legal action to protect or enforce IP rights may result in significant costs and resource diversion, with no guarantee of success.
peer_risks.why: Suits or proceedings to enforce IP rights could incur substantial attorney fees, divert management attention, and the company may not prevail in such actions.

peer_risks.name: Regulatory impacts from global climate change laws and GHG emissions requirements
peer_risks.description: New or expanded climate regulations could increase production costs through energy taxes, emissions permits, or renewable mandates.
peer_risks.why: Governments have adopted or are contemplating regulations on carbon emissions, GHG reporting, and energy use, which could raise production costs and prevent passing price increases to customers.

peer_risks.name: Inability to compete due to differing global climate regulations
peer_risks.description: Companies in jurisdictions without climate regulations may gain competitive advantage over VALHI’s operations in regulated regions.
peer_risks.why: Future climate laws could negatively impact VALHI’s or its customers’/suppliers’ ability to compete with companies in areas not subject to such regulations.

peer_risks.name: Global operational risks from economic, political, and regulatory instability
peer_risks.description: International operations face risks from trade barriers, sanctions, conflicts, and inconsistent legal enforcement.
peer_risks.why: Operations in multiple countries expose the company to trade barriers, tariffs, economic sanctions, armed conflicts (e.g., Russia-Ukraine, Israel-Hamas), and difficulties enforcing legal rights.

peer_risks.name: Technology failures and cybersecurity breaches disrupting operations
